titel: The costs of a home in the US
kurz: The purchase price is only one of three amounts that decide a home purchase, and the only one shown in the listing.

bloecke.md: Three amounts decide a home purchase. The first is the purchase price shown in the listing. The second is the closing costs. They fall due on the day of closing, are lost once paid and do not reappear in any appraisal of the house. The third amount is the cost of keeping the house: property tax, insurance and maintenance. It arises over decades, and only part of it is in any contract. Maintenance in particular is not invoiced by anyone until something breaks, which is why it is regularly set at zero. Over the years, these running costs add up to a multiple of the closing costs.

## One-off closing costs

Federal law makes the closing costs visible early. Under the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule, the lender must send a **Loan Estimate** within three business days of receiving a mortgage application, and a **Closing Disclosure** at least three business days before closing (12 CFR 1026.19). Both use the same standard form, so the figures can be compared line by line and between lenders.

The costs fall into a few groups. The lender charges origination or underwriting fees and, if you choose to buy them, discount points, each costing 1% of the loan amount. Third parties are paid for the appraisal, the title search, the settlement or escrow agent and title insurance. Lender's title insurance protects the lender and is practically always required; owner's title insurance protects the buyer against defects in the title, such as old liens or errors in earlier transfers, and is a one-time premium paid at closing. Local governments charge recording fees and, in many states, transfer taxes. On top of this come prepaid items, such as the first year of homeowners insurance and interest up to the first payment date, and the initial deposit into the escrow account. These are not costs in the strict sense, because they pay for later periods, but they have to be brought to closing in cash.

bloecke.md:
All amounts in the table are assumptions for illustration. Who pays which item, and how much, differs widely. Transfer taxes range from zero in states that do not levy one to several percent in some states and cities, sometimes with higher rates for expensive homes, and local custom decides whether buyer or seller pays them. Title insurance premiums are regulated or even set by the state in many states. In some states, an attorney must take part in the closing.

The agent's commission is mostly a selling cost in the US, but it can also affect buyers. Since August 17, 2024, under the practice changes that followed the settlement of the National Association of Realtors, buyers working with a Realtor must sign a written agreement with their agent before touring a home, and offers of buyer-agent compensation may no longer be published in the multiple listing service. The commission was never fixed by law. Historically, total commissions of around 5% to 6% of the sale price were common, usually paid by the seller out of the proceeds. Today, how much the buyer's agent receives, and who pays it, is agreed in each case and is negotiable.

bloecke.titel: From purchase price to all-in cost
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a purchase price of $400,000 with the closing costs from the table. Closing costs amount to $12,000 or 3.0% of the price; the prepaid items are not included because they pay for later periods.

bloecke.md:
The lender bases the loan on the lower of the purchase price and the appraised value, not on the total cost of the purchase. Closing costs do not increase the value of the house and must therefore be paid in cash or paid for in another way. A seller credit is usually reflected in a higher purchase price, and a lender credit is paid for with a higher interest rate over the life of the loan.

In the example, the buyer needs $80,000 for a 20% down payment, $12,000 in closing costs and $4,500 in prepaid items and escrow deposit, a total of $96,500. A buyer with $100,000 in savings is left with $3,500 after closing. That is less than two monthly payments for principal, interest, tax and insurance, and the first repair is only a matter of time.

bloecke.titel: Market value and break-even sale price over time
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation based on the all-in cost of $412,000. After selling costs of 6%, a sale only recovers the all-in cost at a price of about $438,300. At an assumed price increase of 1% a year, the market value only reaches this after just over nine years; at 3% a year, after just over three. The growth rates are assumptions, not forecasts.

bloecke.md:
The chart is an arithmetical check, not a forecast. As long as the market value is below the dashed line, a sale would mean a loss, even if the price has risen. Because a sale before this point is expensive, owning a home is illiquid.

The closing costs are not entirely lost for tax purposes. For a home you live in, settlement costs such as title insurance, recording fees and transfer taxes paid by the buyer are added to the cost basis and reduce the taxable gain when you sell, which matters if the gain exceeds the Section 121 exclusion. Points paid on a mortgage to buy a main home can generally be deducted as interest, and property tax paid at closing counts as property tax, but both only help if you itemize. For a rental property, the acquisition costs become part of the basis of the building and are recovered through depreciation; the part attributable to the land is not depreciated.

## Running costs

**Property tax** is a local tax, levied by counties, cities, school districts and other local bodies, and in most places it is the largest running cost after the mortgage. It is calculated as assessed value times the tax rate, often stated in mills, that is, dollars per $1,000 of assessed value. An assessed value of $360,000 at a combined rate of 12.5 mills, or 1.25%, results in $4,500 a year. Many states offer homestead exemptions for owner-occupiers, and some cap the annual increase in assessed value. In California, Proposition 13 limits the general tax rate to 1% of assessed value plus voter-approved levies and limits increases in assessed value to 2% a year until the property is sold. In many states, the assessment is reset at sale, so the buyer's tax bill can be considerably higher than the one the seller paid.

In addition, there is homeowners insurance, which lenders require. Standard policies do not cover flood. If the house is in a special flood hazard area and the mortgage comes from a federally regulated or insured lender, flood insurance is mandatory. For a condominium or a house in a planned community, there are HOA dues, which fund the common areas and a reserve. Most lenders collect property tax and insurance through an **escrow account**: each month, one twelfth of the expected annual bills is added to the payment, and the servicer reviews the account once a year. If tax or premiums rise, the monthly payment rises with them, even with a fixed-rate loan.

punkte: Private mortgage insurance or FHA mortgage insurance, if the down payment is small
Flood insurance, where the lender requires it
HOA or condo dues and any special assessments
Replacement of major components: roof, heating and cooling system, water heater
Utilities, which the owner pays in full
Lawn care, snow removal, pest control
A cash reserve for all of the above

bloecke.md: For owners, this split has no influence on the total, because they pay both columns. But it explains why the figure lenders and online calculators call the monthly payment, often abbreviated as PITI for principal, interest, taxes and insurance, is not the cost of owning. The right-hand column is missing from it, and with it the items that make the difference between a home that is affordable and one that only looks affordable.

## Maintenance and reserves

A building wears out. Roof, windows, heating and air conditioning, plumbing and wiring, siding and bathrooms have a limited lifespan, and the costs of renewing them arise irregularly, often in five-figure amounts. Whether money has been set aside for this makes no difference to when they fall due. For a single-family house, no law requires a reserve. For condominiums and HOAs, state laws differ: some require reserve studies or minimum funding, many do not. After the collapse of a condominium building in Surfside in 2021, Florida tightened its rules for structural inspections and reserves of condominium buildings.

There are two common rules of thumb for the amount. One is 1% of the purchase price a year, the other $1 per square foot of living space a year. Both are conventions without a legal basis. A third approach comes from reserve studies, which associations use: list the major components, estimate their replacement cost and remaining life, and save the corresponding share each year.

bloecke.formel: Annual reserve = Σ Replacement cost of component / Useful life of component
bloecke.erklaerung: The component method spreads each expected replacement over its useful life. It is the logic behind professional reserve studies. Its result is only as good as the assumed costs and lifespans, which differ by region, quality and climate.
variablen: today's cost of renewing the component, including labor
assumed total life in years; for a used house, the remaining life matters for timing, not for the annual amount
bloecke.beispiel: Assumed costs and lifespans for a house of 2,000 square feet: roof $15,000 / 25 years = $600; heating and air conditioning $12,000 / 15 = $800; water heater $1,800 / 12 = $150; exterior paint $7,000 / 10 = $700; windows $20,000 / 30 = $667; appliances $6,000 / 12 = $500; flooring $12,000 / 20 = $600. Total about $4,017 a year, before smaller repairs.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a house of 2,000 square feet with a purchase price of $400,000. The square-foot rule gives half of what the other two give, which is why every figure quoted needs a statement of which convention is meant.
kategorien: Rule of thumb: 1% of purchase price

bloecke.md: There are arguments for each convention. The square-foot rule ignores the age and quality of the house and the local price level for labor. The 1% rule scales with the price, which in expensive areas mainly reflects the land, not the building, so it can overstate maintenance there and understate it in cheap areas with old houses. The component method is the most precise, but it relies on assumptions about costs and lifespans that nobody knows exactly for a used house. In practice, all three serve as a floor for ongoing repairs, not as a budget for a major renovation.

A low reserve does not lower the costs; it postpones them. In a condominium or HOA, the missing amount is collected through a special assessment, in one sum and on a date that the owner does not determine. In a single-family house, it arrives as a repair bill. Both typically come at a time when contractors are busy and prices are high.

There is no official checklist, but there is a useful order. What to ask for is the year of the last replacement, not the condition, in each case with receipts or permits:

- Heating, ventilation and air conditioning, including the age of the outdoor unit
- Roof covering, gutters and flashing
- Windows and exterior doors
- Electrical panel and wiring, with the panel's age and capacity
- Supply and drain lines, including the sewer line to the street, which a camera inspection can check
- Foundation, drainage, siding and decks

A professional home inspection, made a condition of the purchase contract through an inspection contingency, is the usual way to find problems before closing. Building permits on file with the city or county show which work was done officially. If several components reach the end of their lifespan at the same time, the costs add up. A house whose components all date from the same decade is therefore riskier than one that has been worked on in stages.

## Disclosures and legal obligations

Most states require sellers to disclose known material defects, often on a standard form, but the scope differs from state to state, and in some states the principle that the buyer must inspect still largely applies. One rule is federal: for housing built before 1978, the seller must disclose known lead-based paint hazards, hand over an EPA information pamphlet and give the buyer ten days to have a lead inspection carried out, unless the buyer waives this right.

There is no nationwide energy performance certificate. Some cities require energy disclosures or ratings for certain buildings, and a home energy audit can be commissioned privately. For estimating costs, the utility bills of the last twelve months are the most useful information, keeping in mind that they reflect the habits of the previous occupants. The federal tax credits for energy-efficient home improvements (Section 25C) and residential clean energy (Section 25D) ended for property placed in service, or expenditures made, after December 31, 2025, so they should no longer be counted on.

bloecke.titel: Obligations that come with the purchase
bloecke.md:
Some costs only arise because ownership changes. The most important is property tax reassessment: where the assessment is reset at sale, the tax is calculated from your purchase price, not from the seller's old assessed value. Ask the county assessor or use its estimator before you calculate the payment.

In addition, some states and cities attach requirements to a sale, such as smoke and carbon monoxide detectors that meet current rules, a municipal resale inspection or certificate of occupancy, or an inspection of the sewer line. Work that the previous owner did without a permit becomes the buyer's problem: the city can require it to be permitted, corrected or removed. If the house is in a special flood hazard area, flood insurance becomes mandatory with the new mortgage, even if the seller never had it. A seller who correctly says they never had to deal with any of this is only describing their own situation, not that of the buyer.

- Title commitment with its exceptions (easements, liens, restrictions) and, where common, a survey
- Seller's disclosure statement and, for houses built before 1978, the lead-based paint disclosure
- Home inspection report and receipts or permits for the six expensive components
- For a condominium or HOA, also the governing documents, the budget, the reserve study or reserve balance, the minutes of recent meetings and any planned special assessments
- The current property tax bill and an estimate of the tax after reassessment
- Insurance quotes including flood and, where relevant, wind coverage, and the Loan Estimate compared with the Closing Disclosure line by line

mitnehmen: Closing costs typically come to around 2% to 5% of the price, depending on state, lender and local custom; they do not increase the value of the house and must be paid in cash or through a higher price or interest rate.
The Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure show all costs on a standard form and make offers comparable line by line.
Property tax is local and can be reset at sale, so the seller's tax bill says little about the buyer's.
The monthly payment that lenders quote (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) leaves out maintenance, HOA dues, special assessments and utilities.
Maintenance conventions differ by a factor of two; the component method shows which replacements are coming and when.

begriffe.text: Fees and taxes paid at the closing of a home purchase, such as lender fees, appraisal, title insurance, recording fees and transfer taxes, typically around 2% to 5% of the price. Prepaid items and escrow deposits are paid at closing as well but are not costs in the strict sense.

Insurance against losses from defects in the title, such as undisclosed liens or errors in earlier transfers. The lender's policy protects the lender and is usually required; the owner's policy protects the buyer. Both are paid once, at closing.

Account kept by the loan servicer from which property tax and insurance are paid. The borrower pays one twelfth of the expected annual amount with each mortgage payment, and the account is reviewed once a year.
Tax levied by some states, counties and cities when real estate changes hands, calculated on the price. Rates and who pays differ by location; some states levy none.

Money set aside for the future renewal of major components. For a house, it is voluntary; for condominiums and HOAs, state law may require reserve studies or minimum funding. A reserve that is too low leads to special assessments.
